thread.title: Small businesses struggle with job vacancies despite efforts to hire
thread.title_full: Small businesses struggle with job vacancies despite efforts to hire

author: Centennial State News
title: Small businesses struggle with job vacancies despite efforts to hire
text:
Daniel J. Block NFIB/Colorado Leadership Council | Official Website
Daniel J. Block NFIB/Colorado Leadership Council | Official Website
In June, small business owners continued to face challenges in filling job openings, as revealed by the latest report from the National Federation of Independent Business (NFIB). According to the report, 36% of small business owners reported unfilled job openings, a two-point increase from May.
Chief Economist Bill Dunkelberg noted that despite a slowing labor market, "many small business owners are still looking to attract applicants and hire for their open positions." He added that "compensation pressures remain strong for those owners who are competing to retain and attract talent in their business."
While specific state data is not available, NFIB State Director Michael Smith highlighted the difficulties faced by businesses in Colorado. “Our members want to create more jobs for Coloradans, but the right applicants are in short supply. That makes it more difficult for Main Street employers to plan for the future and grow their businesses, which affects the local economy,” Smith stated.
The report showed that 58% of small business owners were hiring or attempting to hire in June, an increase of three points from May. However, half of these owners reported having few or no qualified applicants for their positions. Specifically, 25% reported few qualified candidates and another 25% found none at all.
Job openings were most prevalent in construction, manufacturing, and transportation industries. Conversely, finance and agriculture saw fewer openings. A net 13% of business owners planned to create new jobs over the next three months.
Labor quality remained a concern with 16% of owners citing it as their top operational issue. Labor costs emerged as a growing concern too, increasing one point from May to 10%.
On compensation trends, a seasonally adjusted net 33% of small business owners increased wages in June—marking the largest monthly rise since January 2020. Looking ahead, a net 19% plan further compensation hikes within three months.
The full NFIB Jobs Report can be accessed online.
